doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Quitting engineering for full-time music in the 1970s
summary: After a few years in engineering, a failing first marriage and meeting his wife, Red Balaban's salary offer and Benny Goodman's call made music viable.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: It was a good answer. When it came down to making a living when you were a young man, you were going to take a crack at being a full time musician.

Oh yeah. This came after I worked for a couple of years in engineering and purchasing, yeah. That was my midlife crisis see. A lot of very fortunate things happened to me at that time. I guess I was in my late 30s and my first marriage, which was very good for several years, sort of petered out as I got more and more involved in music and less and less involved with a business career and the success thing which I think my ex-wife expected me to do. In all fairness to her she married a Princeton grad and probably thought I would put away childish things like playing jazz. But that didn’t happen. So at the time our marriage was breaking up I met my present wife who has been a constant, reinforcing my career. She graduated college and majored in speech pathology but ended up singing with a band also. So I met her on a gig, I was subbing for the regular trumpet

player. And so since then I’ve had this strength behind me to get into music. You know what I’m saying. This massive move to give up my day job and get into music wasn’t done alone, it was done with a lot of help. Also my ex-partner, Red Balaban, who I’d been working with when I quit my day job, he put me on a partial salary to go out and book his band, Balaban and Cats. Just at that very time Benny Goodman called me and said, “Hey Ed this is Benny.” I said, “Who’s this?” “Benny.” “Benny?” “Benny Goodman,” he said, “can you make a rehearsal next week?” I said, “Well you don’t even know how I play.” He says, “Well Bobby Hackett just recommended you to me,” and he said, “if it’s good enough for Bobby it’s good enough for me.” I show up at a rehearsal with Benny Goodman. This is all happening it was like about one year’s time where I quit my day job, my marriage is coming to an end, I met my future wife, and I see that possibly I have economically a way of making it as a full time musician. Balaban ends up being my partner at Eddie Condon’s and I eventually buy into the club and become manager and part owner. I worked with Benny Goodman and I’m getting fame within certain parameters. And so becoming a full time musician, even in the middle, it was the mid-1970s this happened, so I’m out of school now fifteen years by this time this is happening. In the 60s it would have been a disaster to get into music full time playing the music that I loved. Rock had taken over completely and there were only six clubs in all of New York City that featured jazz of any kind that was going on. I was promoting stuff in New Jersey at the time. So that was the transition into music full time. I don’t know if that was what you had intended me to say.
Yeah. That a certain number of things happened to come together that allowed you to do that.
